title: Accelerating Quantum Dense-Output Simulation through Locality
authors: Songqinghao Yang, Chang Liu, Junkai Wang, Jingxuan Zhang, Jin-Peng Liu
abstract: Estimating time-accumulated observables, or dense outputs, is central to extracting classical information from quantum simulations. Whereas most quantum-simulation algorithms aim to reproduce a final state or a single-time expectation value, many applications require the integrated signal $J_H(O)=\int_0^T \langle ψ(t)|O(t)|ψ(t)\rangle\,dt$. Previous Hamiltonian-simulation-based dense-output algorithms have query costs that depend on the norm of the full Hamiltonian, which can grow with system size. However, one can naturally optimize the simulation algorithm when the system structure is known. Consequently, we develop a locality-based truncation framework for the dense-output problem on lattice Hamiltonians. By truncating the Hamiltonian and tightening the resulting error with Lieb-Robinson bounds, we show that a local simulation can recover the dense output. We bound the quantum simulation error from spatial truncation and translate it into local-simulation query bounds. Our analysis includes free and interacting systems for both fermions and bosons, as well as open quantum systems governed by Lindbladians. The improvement from our truncation algorithm varies from constant to unbounded as the system size grows. We also give example applications and conduct relevant numerical experiments to support our findings.
summary: This paper introduces a locality-based framework to accelerate the simulation of time-accumulated observables (dense outputs) in quantum many-body systems. By leveraging Lieb-Robinson bounds, the authors demonstrate that restricting the simulation to a local region around the observable is sufficient to achieve high accuracy. This significantly reduces computational resource requirements, making simulations of large, complex lattice models more feasible.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently estimating time-accumulated observables (dense outputs) in quantum simulations, which traditionally requires resources scaling with the full Hamiltonian norm.
main_result: By developing a locality-based truncation framework utilizing Lieb-Robinson bounds, the authors show that local simulation resources can recover the dense output, leading to query complexity that can be independent of the total system size.
method: The core method involves spatially truncating the Hamiltonian to a local region and rigorously bounding the resulting error using Lieb-Robinson bounds, which are then translated into local-simulation query bounds.
model_or_system: The analysis applies to quantum many-body systems on a lattice, covering free and interacting fermionic and bosonic models, as well as open quantum systems governed by Lindbladians.
key_observables: Dense Output: $\mathcal{J}_H(O) = \int_0^T \langle \psi(t)|O(t)|\psi(t)angle dt$; Local-simulation query bounds.
important_parameters: Evolution time $T$, target precision $\epsilon$, system size $N$, and the decay exponent $\alpha$ governing Hamiltonian locality.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the existence of spatial locality bounds (Lieb-Robinson bounds) and the ability to truncate the Hamiltonian while maintaining controlled error bounds.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of the required local region on simulation time and precision, and demonstrate the resource improvement by comparing local vs. full Hamiltonian norms.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of dense output estimation, introduces the locality-based truncation framework using LRBs, provides theoretical bounds for various lattice systems (fermions/bosons/open systems), and concludes with numerical verification and complexity analysis.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial theoretical tool for simulating large, complex quantum systems by proving that local information access is sufficient for calculating time-integrated observables, which is vital for simulating dynamics in condensed matter systems.
